Complementary information — Multiple sources agree on improvement but add different details on prevalence, timing, and exceptions.

The evidence clusters by agreement on the core fact that RA often improves during pregnancy (d1, d2, d4, d7, d9), with d3, d5, d6, and d8 adding complementary nuances about variability, timing (e.g., third trimester), and the fact improvement is not universal. All documents are non-contradictory; they provide different facets of the same general answer.

The supporting documents (d1, d2, d4, d7, d9) decisively state that RA improves for a majority of patients during pregnancy, with specific percentages (70-80%, >75%). The partially supporting documents add context: improvement is frequent but not universal (d3, d6), some patients remain active (d5), and the observation is linked to hormonal changes (d8). Together, they form a coherent, multi-faceted answer.

Yes, pregnancy often improves Rheumatoid Arthritis symptoms for a majority of patients. Multiple sources report that 70% to 80% [d1] or more than three quarters [d7] of women with RA experience improved symptoms during pregnancy, and it has long been established that the disease improves in this period [d2, d4]. However, this improvement is not universal, as joint symptoms frequently but not always remit [d6], and a significant portion of patients may still have active disease [d5]. The symptomatic relief is often noted in the later stages of pregnancy [d7] and is linked to immunological and hormonal changes [d4, d9].
